item.title: This Anker 7-in-1 USB-C hub is under $25, which is the lowest it has been in a year
item.itunes:title: This Anker 7-in-1 USB-C hub is under $25, which is the lowest it has been in a year
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Thin laptops have made port versatility a luxury, and a good USB-C hub is the easiest fix. The Anker 7-in-1 USB-C hub is now $24.46 on Amazon, which is just $0.47 above its all-time low and well below its typical $38-40 range. If you're working with a laptop that only has one or two USB-C ports, this hub solves the port shortage without adding bulk. It's the kind of accessory you grab once and forget about.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Anker USB-C 7-in-1 hub

Anker's USB-C 7-in-1 hub isn't strictly just for laptops. It can also be used with other devices as well, like the Steam Deck, smartphones, tablets, and more. It features two USB 3.0 ports, an HDMI output, a USB-C data port, and an SD and microSD card reader.

See at Amazon

A compact way to expand any laptop

The Anker 7-in-1 hub packs 4K HDMI and two USB-A 3.0 ports into a single, compact device. It also has two USB-C ports, an SD and microSD card slot.

It's designed for people who need to connect a monitor, mouse, keyboard, and storage drive without a tangle of adapters. We've covered USB-C hubs before, and the Anker 7-in-1 stands out for its build quality and port selection at this price point.

It's not the most feature-packed hub on the market, but for most laptop users, it covers the essentials without being overkill. You can even use it for other products as well, like smartphones, PC gaming handhelds, and home labs.

The 4K HDMI output makes it a solid option for connecting an external monitor, and the SD card slots are a welcome addition for photographers or video editors who still rely on physical media.

You also get pass-through charging, with 100W going into the USB-C hub and 85W going out to the connected device. It's compatible with a range of different products like Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and more.

But you'll want to check with the product page to ensure your device is truly supported. At $24.46, this is within $0.47 of the lowest price, making it a no-brainer if you need a reliable USB-C hub. Grab it while it's on sale.

item.title: Your ISP's router may let your provider log in and change settings whenever it wants
item.itunes:title: Your ISP's router may let your provider log in and change settings whenever it wants
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Often, times when you plug in an ISP-provided gateway or router, you are rarely the sole administrator of your own local network hardware. Behind the scenes, a lot of major internet service providers utilize standardized remote management protocols, most notably the CPE WAN Management Protocol (CWMP). This is widely known as TR-069, in order to maintain, configure, and troubleshoot your equipment without requiring a physical service call.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

While this mechanism enables seamless zero-touch provisioning and automated firmware delivery, it also gives your provider a persistent communication pipeline to log in, inspect device parameters, and change configurations on demand. For technical users and home lab enthusiasts, understanding how this protocol operates exposes the boundary between convenience and local network sovereignty.

Your ISP router is the biggest bottleneck in your home network, and you know it

It's high time you replaced your ISP's router with something better

By  Tanveer Singh

The technical architecture

How do auto-configuration servers work?

The TR-069 protocol establishes a standardized framework between the customer premises equipment (essentially the hardware your ISP provides, like your gateway or router) and an auto-configuration server known as an ACS, which the provider manages.

Communications within standard CWMP are fundamentally device-initiated. Your router will periodically check in with the provider's ACS using an interval defined as the periodic inform interval and then transmit a standard inform message over HTTP or HTTPS.

Outside of these periodic inform intervals, there can also be connection requests. To initiate changes outside the schedule, the ACS can send a connection request to a specific local or public endpoint on the router (prompting the CPE to immediately open a new management session and pull down updated configuration parameters).

Protocols rely on structured data trees, such as TR-098 or the modern TR-181 standard, which expose thousands of distinct device parameters ranging from WAN IP configurations and DNS settings to connected Wi-Fi client telemetry.

What can your ISP actually modify?

They don't even need to dispatch a technician

Your internet service provider can modify a range of different settings and operational features remotely. Upon a first boot or a factory reset, the gateway will query the ACS to pull down broadband credentials, VLAN identifiers, and VoIP profiles, allowing your internet service provider to ship pre-configured hardware that provisions itself upon connection.

Beyond this, you'll likely have silent firmware upgrades as your internet service provider will maintain control over your device firmware life cycles. This means that critical security patches, bug fixes, or carrier-specific software updates are pushed directly via the ACS, frequently executing reboots without requiring explicit consent from you.

Network engineers can also remotely inspect or alter your Wi-Fi SSID, encryption keys, channel widths, and firewall rules to troubleshoot any connection issues or optimize upstream node performance without dispatching a technician. The ACS can trigger active diagnostics such as line testing and speed diagnostics, which can harvest deep performance metrics to diagnose local line degradation or equipment faults.

Stop trusting your ISP's router blindly

Several grave dangers lurk

8
By  Chandraveer Mathur

There's a range of security implications

But luckily, there are solutions to the issue

Credit: 

While all of this sounds great in theory (since, on the surface, it's just your internet service provider troubleshooting and pushing fundamental firmware updates), there are security implications and boundaries that feel like they're being crossed because TR-069 endpoints listen for connection requests. Sometimes, misconfigured or poorly implemented combined TR-064/TR-069 interfaces have historically been targeted by botnets and automated exploits looking to hijack vulnerable routers over the public internet. This feature can make your home network have a much easier-to-target attack surface.

With some consumer gateways, you can actually be locked out from modifying core network features (such as custom DNS routing, local routing tables, or advanced firewall toggles), despite the fact that you are the administrator and you're paying for a service. This is because it effectively prioritizes centralized operator control over your own user customization. While this isn't true for all routers, it is for some.

For power users seeking to reclaim autonomy, configuring the ISP gateway into bridge mode or IP pass-through can disable its internal routing, DHCP, and wireless capabilities, handing off a public IP assignment and routing duties to an independent user-owned firewall or router. Bridge mode doesn't necessarily stop remote management. In many setups, the ISP gateway still contacts the ACS on a management interface even when its routing, DHCP, and Wi-Fi are disabled.

Outside of this, you can adopt independent hardware altogether. Replacing your ISP-provided gateway entirely with an independent modem, ONT, or mesh Wi-Fi system running open-source or fully auditable firmware can ensure that remote configuration pathways are entirely under local administration. Double-check if this is possible, as some ISPs restrict third-party modems or require their own device for voice or TV.

You don't need to stick to your ISP router

An alternative might serve you better

The reality of modern broadband deployment means that convenience often comes bundled with remote vendor access. While TR-069 and its modern successor (TR-369) remain indispensable operational backbones for telecommunications providers managing millions of subscriber endpoints, they fundamentally shift device control away from you as the end user.

Understanding how these background management loops operate empowers technical users to take deliberate steps, such as implementing bridge configurations or deploying independent networking hardware. That way, you can ensure sovereignty over your local environment. But there is another way. Build your own firewall and router with a mini PC and custom software.

5 reasons an old PC is better than any consumer firewall you can buy

Why waste money on an enterprise firewall when you can build your own from old PC parts?

5

item.title: We almost didn't believe how cheap this 4K streaming stick from Amazon is right now
item.itunes:title: We almost didn't believe how cheap this 4K streaming stick from Amazon is right now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Streaming quality is a top priority for many users, and the Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K is the most efficient way to upgrade your viewing experience without spending a fortune. Right now, it is available for $19.99 on Amazon, which is its all-time lowest price and one we almost didn't believe was real. This is a significant drop from its usual cost, making it an exceptional value for anyone looking to add 4K and HDR to their setup.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The device is compact, measuring just 3.9 inches in length, and connects directly to your TV via HDMI. It supports 4K resolution, HDR10, and HLG, ensuring that your content looks as good as it did when it was produced. The 1.7GHz processor is 25% faster than the previous generation, which helps the interface feel snappy and responsive during navigation. It can run a bunch of available apps and can even stream from Plex, Jellyfin, and other self-hosted services.

Simply plug one of these discounted Fire TV 4K sticks into your TV, and you'll have access to the best streaming services (including your own self-hosted media!) and much more.

Why this is the best 4K streaming option

One of the standout features is the inclusion of Wi-Fi 6, which provides a more stable and faster connection compared to standard Wi-Fi 5. This is crucial for maintaining high-quality streams without buffering, especially if other devices on your network are consuming bandwidth. The remote is also an improvement, featuring a dedicated Alexa button and an infrared blaster that allows you to control compatible AV receivers and soundbars directly from the stick's remote.

While the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus and Max offer slightly higher performance with Wi-Fi 6E and a 2.0GHz processor (as well as Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos), the difference in real-world usage is minimal for most users. The standard 4K model handles 4K HDR content effortlessly and is the best choice for those who want a reliable, affordable streaming solution. At $19.99, the Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is an easy recommendation. It delivers premium features like 4K HDR at a price point that is hard to beat. This is a rare opportunity to grab a high-quality streaming device at its lowest ever price, so it is worth considering if you are looking to upgrade your entertainment system. If you're able to pick one up for $20, congratulations... we're happy for you and not at all salty about paying more for ours.

item.title: Unix pipes are over 50 years old, and they're still why the Linux terminal feels so powerful
item.itunes:title: Unix pipes are over 50 years old, and they're still why the Linux terminal feels so powerful
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One of the coolest parts of computing is discovering that the tech you're interacting with on a daily basis was invented decades before your PC even existed. One of them kicks in whenever you use the terminal, and while you don't see them working away in the background, you can invoke them at any time. It's the humble pipe, and its invention starts with a note all the way back in the 60s.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The pipe began with the desire to make a digital garden hose

The final name didn't deviate too far from the idea of liquid transit

In 1964, Douglas McIlroy (the visionary department head for Bell Labs) had a problem. Back then, programs were pretty monolithic; they didn't come with the ability to naturally share data between two programs. Instead, you had to manually write code that would translate data from Program A to Program B. If you wanted to perform a sequence of actions, that would involve a lot of work chaining together these individual tools to get the job done. It was rough work.

On October 11, 1964, Doug McIlroy had had enough. In a memo titled "What's most important," he had an idea as to how things could be better:

“We should have some ways of coupling programs like garden hose – screw in another segment when it becomes necessary to massage data in another way. This is the way of IO also.”

The good news is, McIlroy was on the money; such a system would make it a lot easier to perform tasks that are linked together. The bad news is, Doug McIlroy had to pester Ken Thompson, a Unix co-creator who joined in 1966, for years until he finally caved and added the pipe() system call in February 1973 after a night of coding.

They were pretty much a hit from day one. McIlroy recalls what the first day with pipes looked like at Bell Labs, stunned that all the chaining together they had been doing for years could now be achieved with a single line. Because pipes could pass out data via their stdout data channel and take in data using the stdin channel, you could daisy-chain them and have data flow through each command, much like a hose.

The very next month, in March 1973, McIlroy asked Thompson to "lift the regular expression recognizer out of [an] editor" and turn it into a program he could invoke anywhere. The next day, Thompson created global regular expression print, or 'grep' for short; a command we still use today!

Running Windows apps on Linux just changed forever, and I was one of the first to try it

Things are diferent now

34
By  João Carrasqueira

The new, fancy pipe technology showed up the old ways

The moment when a dinosaur was shown for what it is

The elegance of pipes would be put into the spotlight in 1986, when Jon Bentley, who owned a column called "Programming Pearls" in the publication "Communications of the ACM," asked programmer Donald Knuth to write a program that would take in text, count the most frequently used words, then rank them in order alongside their occurrences.

Knuth got to work, and when he came back, he had over ten pages of Pascal code to get the job done. His code was passed over to McIlroy for critique, who praised Knuth's program and said it was very clever, despite having a few bugs.

He then proceeded to completely obliterate Knuth's program with the following proposal:

tr -cs A-Za-z ' ' |

tr A-Z a-z |

sort |

uniq -c |

sort -rn |

sed ${1}q

Using pipes, he could split words onto separate lines, lowercase everything, sort them alphabetically, count all the duplicates, sort them by frequency, and grab the top few entries of the list. It fits on a Post-It Note, and it became a famous example of how pipes helped people do more, quicker, with less effort.

AI coding agents made me a better programmer, but only after I stopped letting them write the code

Don't let coding agents completely steer your ship.

3
By  Anurag Singh

The pipes still put in work today

The plumbing still works

So, where are those pipes now? Well, they're still being used daily, and there's a good chance you'll use them at least once in your life if you use Linux—much more so if your job or hobby requires lots of terminal commands. For instance, if a Linux user wanted to find the process ID for nginx, they'd open the terminal and type:

ps aux | grep nginx

The "ps aux" part grabs every running process, and "grep nginx" finds lines containing "nginx" in the output. The pipe connecting the two together allows "ps aux" to hand over the text via stdout so that grep can grab it using stdin and find the target word. All you need is four words and a pipe, and you're golden.

6 Linux command line tricks everyone should know

Level up your Linux CLI experience with these cool tricks

6
By  Ayush Pande

Chaining commands together went from pipe dream to pipe-based reality

The next time you're typing a command into your Linux terminal and you find yourself reaching for the trusty pipe, give a thought for the decades of engineering that went into it. It's a lot easier to write than ten pages of Pascal, that's for sure.

item.title: LiberNovo's Black Friday sale: What the Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow do differently
item.itunes:title: LiberNovo's Black Friday sale: What the Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow do differently
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most office chairs are judged on how many adjustments they offer. Seat height, lumbar depth, armrest position, and headrest angle can all be dialed in until the fit feels right. The catch is that the fit only holds for the posture you set it in. Lean back to take a call or reach across the desk, and the support you spent time setting up can end up in the wrong place.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

LiberNovo builds its chairs around a different idea, which it calls dynamic ergonomics, where the chair adjusts to your movements. Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaign, which the company describes as its largest promotion of the year, covers the Omni and Maxis ranges. The top models in each range, the Omni Pro and the Maxis Airflow, show most clearly what LiberNovo is trying to do, so they're worth considering.

Why one posture isn't enough

Workplace guidance has moved away from the idea of a single correct way to sit. That creates a practical problem. A typical workday moves between focused typing, video calls, reading, and short breaks, often in the same chair. A conventional adjustable chair can be set up well for one of those, but every position change moves you away from that setup. Most people don't stop to readjust, so they either sit with support that no longer fits or stay upright to avoid the problem.

What LiberNovo means by dynamic support

Credit: LiberNovo

Synchro-tilt mechanisms, common on premium office chairs, link the seat and backrest so they recline together at a set ratio. That stops you sliding forward when you lean back, but the headrest and armrests usually stay where they were set. Some high-end chairs go further, with flexing backs or arms that move with the user.

LiberNovo's claim is more specific. Its Dynamic Support System links four contact points (neck, back, arms, and seat) so they move together as you recline. The Bionic FlexFit Backrest is split into eight flexible panels joined by 14 dual-link points and 16 ball joints, which lets different zones of the backrest contour to the spine separately instead of tilting as one surface. None of this relies on a lever or dial. You set the chair up once, and it follows your movement from there.

The company also recommends working with your back supported in a slight recline instead of sitting bolt upright at 90 degrees. Its chairs have five fixed recline positions at 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees, and LiberNovo suggests 115 to 125 degrees for most desk work. It points to research, such as a 1999 study published in Spine, which measured lower pressure inside a lumbar disc when people leaned back against a backrest, while acknowledging that this kind of research looked at healthy volunteers over short periods. LiberNovo does not claim its chairs prevent or treat back pain.

Reclining is also where a static chair tends to struggle. Lean back from 105 to 135 degrees, and the lumbar support often stops lining up with the lower back, the headrest meets the back of the skull instead of the neck, and the elbows lift off the armrests. Keeping all three in contact through the recline is the problem the linked design is meant to solve.

Omni Pro: Built for long sessions at one desk

LiberNovo Omni Pro
Brand
LiberNovo
Material
Gabriel Atlantic fabric, aluminum alloy base
Recline
105 to 160 degrees
Colors
Graphite or Glacier

The LiberNovo Omni Pro is an ergonomic chair built for long sessions at one desk. Its Dynamic Support System links the neck, back, arms and seat, so support follows you through five recline positions, while an eight-panel Bionic FlexFit Backrest contours to the spine. Electric lumbar adjustment, a five-minute OmniStretch sequence and Active AirFlow seat ventilation run from a rechargeable battery.

See at LiberNovo

The Omni Pro sits at the top of the Omni range, which is sized for standard builds. LiberNovo lists a recommended height of 153 to 186 cm (5 ft 0 in to 6 ft 1 in) and a maximum load of 300 lb (136 kg), with a choice of 45 cm or 48 cm seat depth. It's aimed at people who spend long stretches at the same desk, including developers, editors, designers, analysts, and gamers.

Credit: LiberNovo

Lumbar depth is set by an electric motor called ErgoPulse, which moves the lumbar zone in or out until it meets the lower back, so there's no reaching for a knob. The chair also includes OmniStretch, a five-minute motorized stretch sequence that runs in deep recline. LiberNovo describes it as an in-chair stretch and reset, not a treatment.

The other headline feature is Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A centrifugal fan running at 4,000 RPM draws air through a five-layer seat, and a sensor pauses it when you stand up. LiberNovo rates fan noise at under 45 dB. Lumbar adjustment, stretching, and ventilation all run from a 3,000mAh rechargeable battery, which the company says offers up to 36 hours of ventilation on low or up to 9 hours on high when the other motors aren't in use. The chair is upholstered in Gabriel Atlantic fabric from Denmark, sits on an aluminum alloy base, and comes in Graphite or Glacier.

Maxis Airflow: Designed around a larger frame

LiberNovo Maxis Airflow
Brand
LiberNovo
Material
Gabriel Atlantic fabric, aluminum alloy base
Recline
105 to 160 degrees
Maximum Load Weight
Up to 399 lbs

The LiberNovo Maxis Airflow is an ergonomic chair designed around a larger frame rather than scaled up from a standard one. It has a wider backrest, an extended-travel headrest, longer arc-shaped armrests and a 52 cm seat. And a six-spring Controlled Recline System engages progressively by angle and weight. Electric lumbar adjustment, OmniStretch, and Active AirFlow seat ventilation are included.

See at LiberNovo

LiberNovo's argument for the Maxis range is that big-and-tall seating is a geometry problem. Scaling a standard chair up still leaves you with standard proportions, so the headrest can run out of travel before it reaches a taller user's neck, the backrest can be too narrow for broad shoulders, and the seat can be too shallow for long thighs.

Credit: LiberNovo

The Maxis Airflow is built for users from about 5 ft 10 in to 6 ft 7 in (178 to 200 cm) and is rated for up to 399 lb (181 kg). It shares the Omni Pro's dynamic platform, including electric lumbar support, OmniStretch, and Active AirFlow, but changes the dimensions around it. The headrest has extended travel and a U-shaped curve; the backrest is wider with a flared base, and the arc-shaped armrests sit lower and are wider and longer. The seat is 20.5 in (52 cm) deep, with a multi-density cushion that's firmer at the rear and softer at the front edge.

The biggest mechanical difference is the recline. A six-spring Controlled Recline System engages progressively by angle and weight, which is designed to stop the backrest from dropping suddenly under a heavier load. Ventilation runtime is rated at up to 24 hours on low or up to 10 hours on high, using the same 3,000mAh battery capacity as the Omni Pro.

What to know before buying

LiberNovo is upfront about a few limits. The chairs follow your movement, but they don't find your fit for you. The first setup involves four adjustments, in order: lumbar support, armrests, seat height, and neck support. If that initial setup is off, the chair will carry the wrong fit in every position, so it's worth taking your time with it.

Both chairs are powered, so the battery needs charging, and there's a short learning curve with the controls. Anyone who wants a purely mechanical chair can look at the Omni SE or Maxis Manual, which keep the dynamic mechanism without a motor or battery. The Omni Gen and Maxis Electric sit in between, with motorized lumbar and OmniStretch but no seat ventilation. On the Maxis, the 20.5 in (52 cm) seat can press behind the knees of people shorter than about 5 ft 10 in, so it's worth checking against your own height before choosing it.

How LiberNovo's Black Friday sale works

The warm-up period opens on November 9 in the US and Canada and November 10 in the EU and UK, with the main sale starting at midnight local time on November 19 in all four regions. Discounts vary by market and reach up to 42% in the US, 41% in Canada, 44% in the EU and 42% in the UK across the Omni and Maxis ranges.

Eligible purchases come with 30-day price protection against qualifying price changes. Larger orders unlock gifts across three tiers, with the top tier including a travel kit made up of an inflatable neck pillow, an eye mask, and noise-reducing earplugs. An automatic Spend & Save discount is also applied at checkout once an order passes set thresholds, with no code needed. Teams buying five or more chairs can get separate business pricing, with different tiers for orders of 5 to 10 chairs and 11 or more.

Interest-free installments are available through Klarna in the US, EU, and UK, and through Afterpay in Canada. A refer-a-friend link gives 3% to both the referrer and the buyer, and loyalty members earn triple points on eligible orders during the campaign. Between November 10 and 18, site visitors can also enter a giveaway to win a LiberNovo chair, with no purchase required (the giveaway isn't running in Italy).

Offers, eligible models, and stock vary by region, so it's worth checking the details at LiberNovo before buying. Every LiberNovo chair is also backed by a 6-year frame warranty and a 2-year warranty on electronics.

item.title: I stopped blaming wireless Android Auto for random disconnects and found the real culprits
item.itunes:title: I stopped blaming wireless Android Auto for random disconnects and found the real culprits
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have always had a love-hate relationship with wireless Android Auto. On a good day, I can hop into my car, start the engine, and have Google Maps and YouTube Music ready before I even leave the parking lot. On a bad day, it’s a different story. The connection takes forever to establish, music randomly stops playing, or Android Auto disconnects right in the middle of navigation.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Initially, I blamed Google’s software and assumed wireless Android Auto was unreliable by nature. However, I started paying closer attention to when the connection failed, what was running on my phone, and which setting might be interfering, and now my wireless Android Auto is as solid as the wired one.

I was troubleshooting the wrong problem

The restart button wasn’t fixing anything

Whenever wireless Android Auto acted up in my car, I followed the same troubleshooting routine. I would restart my Galaxy S25 Ultra, force-stop Android Auto, toggle Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, or disconnect and re-pair my phone with the infotainment system.

These were the usual fixes I had come across online, and to be fair, they occasionally worked. However, the relief was short-lived. The same connection problems would resurface a few days later, sometimes during the very next drive. I eventually realized I wasn’t actually fixing anything. I was just resetting the connection and hoping the problem wouldn’t return.

Instead of blindly repeating the same troubleshooting steps, I decided to approach the problem differently. I started paying attention to exactly when wireless Android Auto failed and what was happening on my phone at that moment. I also kept an eye on my phone’s battery settings, Wi-Fi behavior, and whether certain features were running in the background. This simple change in approach helped me narrow down the possible causes instead of randomly changing settings.

My phone’s smart features weren’t always helping

Smart connectivity wasn’t always so smart

One of my biggest surprises during my troubleshooting was discovering that some of my phone’s intelligent connectivity features were doing more harm than good. These features are designed to optimize network performance, but they don’t always play nicely with wireless Android Auto. For instance, on my Pixel 8, I disabled Adaptive Connectivity. This feature automatically manages network connections to improve battery life and performance. While it’s useful in everyday situations, I suspected it might be interfering with Android Auto’s wireless connection.

After turning it off, I noticed fewer connection hiccups and a more consistent experience during my drives. I faced something similar on my Galaxy S25 Ultra. Samsung’s Intelligent Wi-Fi settings include options to automatically switch between networks or mobile data depending on connection quality. Since wireless Android Auto relies on a Wi-Fi connection with the head unit, I disabled automatic Wi-Fi switching to eliminate another potential issue.

Again, the difference was noticeable as my wireless Android Auto connection became more stable. Neither change is a guaranteed fix for everyone, but both helped in my experience.

My phone’s background behavior raised questions

Battery savings came with hidden compromises

Another thing I started investigating was how my phone handled apps and background processes. Some Android phones are quite aggressive with battery optimization, and Samsung takes it further with its sleeping and deep sleeping apps features. While these tricks can squeeze extra battery life out of my Galaxy S25 Ultra, I began wondering whether they were also affecting my wireless Android Auto experience.

I started by disabling power-saving mode whenever I used Android Auto. I also went to Samsung’s battery settings and made sure Android Auto wasn’t on the Deep sleeping apps list. I added it to the Never auto-sleeping apps list, where available, so the system wouldn’t restrict background activity.

While I was at it, I reviewed other aggressive battery-saving settings that could interfere with essential connectivity services. My wireless Android Auto connection has become more consistent, especially during longer drives where I rely heavily on Google Maps and YouTube Music. The experience taught me that maximizing battery life isn’t always worth compromising background connectivity.

A cheap secondhand phone now runs Android Auto in my car full-time, and my real phone stays in my pocket

Putting old hardware to good use

9
By  Anurag Singh

I stopped overlooking the infotainment system

My phone wasn’t the only suspect

I was so focused on troubleshooting my phone that I overlooked the car’s infotainment system. After all, wireless Android Auto relies on both devices working together.

I started restarting the head unit, checking the firmware updates, and reviewing its connectivity settings. I also tested another Android phone to see whether the same problems persisted. This helped me narrow down whether the issue came from Android Auto software or the head unit itself.

The connection problems had unexpected origins

I used to blame wireless Android Auto for every random disconnect, but this little investigation changed my perspective. The problem wasn’t always Google’s software. Sometimes, it was my phone’s aggressive battery management, intelligent connectivity features, or even the infotainment system itself. Wireless Android Auto still isn’t flawless, but my connection is more reliable now.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
At this point, most of us already know that frame generation isn't really the same as getting a higher frame rate by lowering settings, using upscaling, or upgrading your hardware. Of course, it does make games look smoother by inserting generated frames between real ones, but those frames won't do anything for the game's responsiveness. Still, as a competitive gamer, I've always wondered just how much responsiveness actually matters in slower, single-player titles.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So I decided to put that to the test in Cyberpunk 2077 using my RTX 4090. item.title: I replaced Task Manager’s GPU tab with a free open-source tool, and finally found where my VRAM was going
item.itunes:title: I replaced Task Manager’s GPU tab with a free open-source tool, and finally found where my VRAM was going
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
VRAM is as good as gold these days, both within the context of high-resolution gaming and running local AI. Knowing where it all goes is important, but on Windows, there's no itemized breakdown of exactly what those applications and processes are doing with that valuable memory, and that's why gputaskman was made. Scott Hanselman, a VP at Microsoft, released gputaskman on GitHub, and it shows exactly which processes are eating up your GPU. It's completely open-source, runs in a terminal, and is invaluable if you handle workloads that touch VRAM.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
A Microsoft engineer finally gives Windows 11 a proper, unofficial GPU monitor

What's using your GPU? Now you can find out.

2
By  Simon Batt

Task Manager tells you how much, but not exactly what it's doing

There's no clear picture as to what your VRAM is actually doing

Task Manager has been able to show how much of your VRAM is being used for years, but it only gives you a couple of numbers to go off of. If I load up a local model in llama.cpp and open a few browser tabs with video elements, the usage will jump, but I have no idea what each load is actually doing with that memory. Local LLMs on consumer GPUs can easily take up all of your VRAM, but it's important to know what else might be leaking into that GDDR memory.

The Performance tab in Task Manger charts dedicated and shared GPU memory for the whole card, and if you add the Dedicated GPU memory column in the Details tab, you get a figure for each process too. On Windows, gputaskman reads from the same family of graphics counters, so the totals line up closely, but you get a much clearer picture of what’s using memory.

gputaskman sorts every process into a type and labels them: LLM, compositor, browser, app or system. It notes which graphics runtime each process is using and adds a short description of what its memory probably holds, if possible. The device panel at the top rolls all of that into one stacked bar, so you can see at a glance how much of the card belongs to the model and how much belongs to everything else.

I ran local LLMs on a "dead" GPU, and the results surprised me

My Pascal card may not be ideal for intensive workloads, but it's more than enough for light LLM-powered tasks

1
By  Ayush Pande

What was actually in my VRAM

I didn't realize my browser took up so much

After I loaded up Qwen3-8B, 7.37GB of my RX 9070 XT's 15.81GB was in use, and more than 4GB of that had nothing to do with the model. The Windows compositor, dwm.exe, was holding 1.37GB, which gputaskman describes as desktop back buffers and compositor surfaces. This, of course, makes a lot of sense, because I run a 4K 240Hz monitor, but I’d never seen it itemized like that before. Brave was using 1.14GB for things like page textures, video and canvas. OBS, which handles my replay buffer for game clips, had 445MB, and Steam’s web helper had 298MB, and a long tail of apps like Discord, Slack and even File Explorer held around a hundred megabytes each.

On a 16GB card that's roughly a quarter of the VRAM capacity gone before the model actually does anything. If you're trying to load a model and it fits via the math but doesn't in reality, check gputaskman before blaming the model.

My RTX Spark laptop rendered a Blender scene too big for an RTX 5090, and a local LLM on the same machine built it

It's not faster than an RTX 5090, but the additional VRAM makes for some cool tricks.

12
By  Adam Conway

The model inspector is the biggest reason to try it

A feature that makes it a must-have

If you select llama-server in the process list, gputaskman will give a bunch of extra detail on top of just the type of process and its usage. It'll identify the model, what architecture it uses, how many parameters, quantization, and the training context. It'll also split the allocation: 4.35GB of weights, 576MB of KV cache and 108MB of compute buffers, the numbers for which are read straight from llama.cpp's logs.

The KV cache amount helps explain a common misread of usage details, and that's why a model can take up more space in VRAM than its file size. gputaskman illustrates this by listing the cost per token, 144KB at the default f16 precision for this model, and does the math for you: 576MB at a 4K context, 4.5GB at 32K. llama.cpp reserves that memory when the model loads.

Without the log file, the KV figures are estimates based on the model file’s metadata. gputaskman can also recognize Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM and Foundry Local out of the box, though the README is upfront that some of those paths have seen less real-world testing than llama.cpp.

Two old GPUs I salvaged are doing more AI work than a brand new $2000 card, and I won't be upgrading anytime soon

I built a local AI setup out of two old GPUs that sell for cheap, and it beats a single new card

4
By  Ayush Pande

It's experimental

You'll probably get more detail than I can if you're on an Nvidia card

  • Credit: Scott Hanselman
  • Credit: Scott Hanselman

This software is a work-in-progress judging by the readme and GitHub history. Things like the device and process counters are measurements but workload labels and model breakdowns are estimates, and may be wrong.

AMD owners on Windows like myself get less detail than Nvidia owners would on their cards. On my RX 9070 XT, memory activity, PCIe traffic and video clock all read N/A, because gputaskman relies on AMD’s driver library there instead of the richer telemetry NVIDIA cards expose.

MoE models changed what "fits on my GPU" means, and most hardware advice hasn't caught up

My 10-year-old GPU runs 26B LLMs now, and MoE models changed everything about LLM-hosting advice

By  Ayush Pande

A no-brainer install for local AI enthusiasts

If you run local models in basically any capacity, gputaskman is a great program to try. It runs on basically every OS and runs directly in a terminal, so its footprint is quite tiny. Compared to Task Manager on Windows, it's a must-have for local AI enthusiasts.

Task Manager tells you how much, but not exactly what it's doing

There's no clear picture as to what your VRAM is actually doing

Task Manager has been able to show how much of your VRAM is being used for years, but it only gives you a couple of numbers to go off of. If I load up a local model in llama.cpp and open a few browser tabs with video elements, the usage will jump, but I have no idea what each load is actually doing with that memory. Local LLMs on consumer GPUs can easily take up all of your VRAM, but it's important to know what else might be leaking into that GDDR memory.

The Performance tab in Task Manger charts dedicated and shared GPU memory for the whole card, and if you add the Dedicated GPU memory column in the Details tab, you get a figure for each process too. On Windows, gputaskman reads from the same family of graphics counters, so the totals line up closely, but you get a much clearer picture of what’s using memory.

gputaskman sorts every process into a type and labels them: LLM, compositor, browser, app or system. It notes which graphics runtime each process is using and adds a short description of what its memory probably holds, if possible. The device panel at the top rolls all of that into one stacked bar, so you can see at a glance how much of the card belongs to the model and how much belongs to everything else.
